titre: The Experiment Voted Most Beautiful in Physics Wasn't the First
accroche: In 2002, a poll names the most beautiful experiment in physics. The name cited dated from 1989; the one who had actually done it in 1976 only resurfaced afterward.
contenu_vulgarise:
In September 2002, the British magazine Physics World asks its readers to name the most beautiful experiment in the history of physics. More than 200 replies come in, and one result dominates by far: the electron-by-electron buildup of an interference pattern through two slits.

## One Grain at a Time, Yet Still a Wave

The experiment stages the most puzzling trait of quantum mechanics. An electron beam so weak that only one electron at a time passes through the apparatus (an electron biprism, standing in for the two slits) should, if it behaved like a marble, produce two spots on the screen, one behind each possible path. Instead, impact after impact, it produces alternating bright and dark bands: the interference pattern characteristic of a wave, built up by grains arriving one at a time, separated in time.

The team that demonstrates this with the greatest impact is Akira Tonomura's, at Hitachi's Advanced Research Laboratory in Tokyo: his 1989 paper, published in the American Journal of Physics, records the pattern's gradual buildup using a position-by-position electron counting system. It is this work that the historical article published by Physics World alongside the 2002 poll presents as the landmark achievement.

## A Letter, a 1976 Film, and a Different Name

Eight months later, in May 2003, physicist John Steeds writes to the magazine: he has seen a 1976 film, shot at the University of Bologna, that already shows the same gradual, electron-by-electron buildup, through a very similar apparatus. Pier Giorgio Merli, Gian Franco Missiroli, and Giulio Pozzi's team had published their results that same year, 1976, in the same journal, the American Journal of Physics, thirteen years before Hitachi. Tonomura's team had never cited this work, apparently unaware of it.

In his reply, Tonomura maintains that his group was the first to observe the pattern building up in real time, from single events. Science historian Rodolfo Rosa, who reconstructed the episode in 2012, concludes without hedging that Merli, Missiroli, and Pozzi carried out the first conclusive double-slit experiment with single electrons.

The experiment voted most beautiful in physics therefore carried, without anyone noticing at the time of the vote, the wrong team's name. It was not the beauty of the result that was in question, only the memory kept of it: thirteen years separate the first demonstration from the one everyone remembered.

repere.texte: In the 2002 Physics World poll, the double-slit experiment with single electrons tops the ranking of the ten experiments selected; the article giving its historical background does not cite the 1976 Bologna work, thirteen years earlier than Hitachi's 1989 paper.
repere.source: Rosa, Rodolfo, “The Merli-Missiroli-Pozzi Two-Slit Electron-Interference Experiment,” Physics in Perspective, 14 (2), 178-195, 2012

carte.punch: The experiment voted most beautiful in physics wasn't the first of its kind
carte.idee: In 2002, a poll names the electron-by-electron buildup of an interference pattern, done by Tonomura's team in 1989, the most beautiful experiment in physics. A 2003 letter reveals that a team in Bologna had published the same demonstration thirteen years earlier, in 1976.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The details of the Bologna apparatus, the 1976 film, and the priority dispute with Hitachi's team.

quiz.question: Why wasn't Hitachi's 1989 experiment, popularized in 2002 as the most beautiful experiment in physics, actually the first of its kind?
choix: Because the 2002 poll was invalidated after a calculation error was found in Tonomura's paper
Because Claus Jönsson had already observed, in 1961, interference with electrons sent one at a time
Because a team in Bologna had published, in 1976, the same electron-by-electron demonstration, thirteen years earlier, in the same journal
Because Tonomura himself admitted to copying the setup of a rival lab without citing it
quiz.explication: The Bologna team (Merli, Missiroli, Pozzi) had published, in 1976, in the same journal as Hitachi, the gradual electron-by-electron buildup of an interference pattern, thirteen years before the paper cited by the 2002 poll. Jönsson, in 1961, sent several electrons at once, not one at a time; the poll was never invalidated, and Tonomura never admitted to copying anyone.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What role does the electron biprism play in Tonomura's apparatus?
choix: It stands in for the two slits, splitting the beam into two possible paths
It amplifies the beam so several electrons pass through at once
It directly counts the number of impacts on the screen
It converts the electrons into photons before the screen
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that the electron biprism stands in for the two slits, leaving two possible paths for a beam so weak that only one electron passes through at a time.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who writes to the magazine, and when, to reveal the existence of the 1976 film shot in Bologna?
choix: Rodolfo Rosa, in his 2012 reconstruction of the episode
John Steeds, in a letter sent to the magazine in May 2003
Peter Rodgers, the author of the article on the poll in 2002
Akira Tonomura, in reply to his own team
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is John Steeds who writes to the magazine in May 2003 to report having seen the 1976 film shot in Bologna, showing the same gradual buildup.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What conclusion does historian Rodolfo Rosa reach in his 2012 reconstruction of the episode?
choix: That the two experiments, thirteen years apart, had in fact taken place the same calendar year
That the 2002 Physics World poll had to be cancelled over a procedural error in the count
That Tonomura's team had knowingly falsified the results published in its 1989 paper
That Merli, Missiroli, and Pozzi had carried out the first conclusive double-slit experiment with single electrons
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Rosa concludes without hedging, in his 2012 reconstruction, that priority belongs to Merli, Missiroli, and Pozzi, whom he credits with the first conclusive double-slit experiment with single electrons.
